CS10-05.note: No sentence states the purpose; it must be assembled from three placed facts - the text sets erosion aside as insufficient to explain the fill ('erosion control asks only for a wall and packed earth'), the fill is graded gravel and coarse sand, and the two observed effects are fast working after rain (drainage) and earlier emergence of sown maize (warming). A is the explanation the text explicitly says is inadequate; B is the reverse of what gravel under topsoil does and is contradicted by the two-day drying; C imports frost heave the text never touches. On the repairer's flag: I AGREE the warming half now rests on the single 'comes up a fortnight earlier' cue, and I agree that cue is not airtight - a solver can attribute earlier emergence to drainage alone, since waterlogging suppresses germination as well as cold does. I put the key's support at roughly three-quarters, same as the repairer. But the weakness does not create a rival: no other option names drainage at all, so the softened half costs the item some precision, not its uniqueness. Worth saying the mechanisms are physically coupled - drained soil is warm soil - so the inference is the one the evidence invites rather than a leap.

CS10-12.note: Requires chaining three facts none of which states the answer: the letters cite a sealed written instrument, no copy survives in EITHER firm's archive, and in the 1438 dispute both houses sent to ONE AND THE SAME chest. A single external repository follows; nothing in the text says 'third party'. C is the strongest distractor and the one I tested hardest - private per-firm ledgers would be a natural way to read 'a division of archives' - but it is closed off twice, by the absence from either archive and by the single shared chest. B and D both restate the Text 1 position (trust, custom) that Text 2 is written against, which is the right kind of trap for a cross-text item. No second defensible reading.

CS10-17.note: Text 2's mechanism is progressive rainout along the air's path - storms 'drop their heaviest water first', so what reaches 'the country beyond' is already stripped, and low modern basins behind young ranges therefore mimic high terrain. C is the only option that names a property of the air's journey rather than of the basin. On the repairer's flag about A: TEMPTING, NOT DEFENSIBLE. The amount effect is real and a solver with isotope knowledge will feel its pull, but A localises it - 'how much rain fell in the seasons when the leaves grew', i.e. rainfall AT the basin - and Text 2's whole point is that the ratio is set upwind, before the air arrives, 'whatever the ground beneath it is doing'. Choosing A reverses the argument. So I dispute nothing about the key, and I would not flag second_defensible. One residual imperfection to record rather than the one flagged: C says 'how far inland', while the text's variable is what the air CROSSED (a mountain front), not raw inland distance - a basin just inland of no relief would not be stripped. C is still uniquely best because it is the only path-of-air option, but the match is by family, not exactly. Separate risk worth naming: A, B and C all name genuine controls on precipitation d18O, so the options do not decide it, but a reader who knows the standard critique of stable-isotope paleoaltimetry (upwind rainout) could reach C without Text 2. I still score passage_needed true - the stem asks what THIS author would say, and only the passage fixes which real control is meant - but this is the item in the set with a live subject-knowledge channel.
